summary: Specifies the Presence Information Data Format, an XML format for presence data used by Common Profile for Presence compliant protocols. It also registers the media type application/pidf+xml for these documents.

eli5.summary: It is a standard note layout for saying whether you are around, so different chat tools can all read the same note.

questions: what does a pidf document look like
subtitle: A small XML format that says whether someone is reachable, readable by any presence system that follows the common profile.

tldr.problem: Different presence and instant messaging systems each described a person's availability in their own way, so presence data could not cross from one system to another unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: PIDF defines an XML document with a presence root holding tuples. Each tuple has a status (open or closed), and optionally a contact address, notes and a timestamp. Extra information is added through XML namespaces.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3863 gives CPP-compliant protocols a shared payload, registered as the application/pidf+xml media type. It defines only the format, not how a protocol carries it.

today: RFC 3863 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the document format and the extension rules; the RFC leaves it to each protocol specification to say how a PIDF document is carried.

sections.title: Why a Common Presence Format
sections.content:
The Common Profiles for Instant Messaging (CPIM) and Presence (CPP) define operations and parameters that let different instant messaging and presence protocols interoperate. RFC 3863 adds the missing piece: the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), a common format for the presence data itself.

With a shared format, presence information can cross the boundary between CPP-compliant protocols without modification. The RFC notes this has benefits for both security and performance.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The memo defines only the payload and its extensibility framework. How a payload travels inside a particular protocol is left to that protocol's own specification, and defining richer status values is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Imagine every school using a different form to say who is in class today. PIDF is one form that everyone agrees to use, so the note makes sense wherever it lands.

sections.title: Design Decisions
sections.content:
The authors started from the presence model in RFC 2778 and the requirements in RFC 2779 and took a minimalist approach: only features needed to solve a particular problem were included.

The minimal model says that presence information consists of one or more presence tuples. A tuple has a status, an optional communication address and optional other markup. Status has at least the mutually exclusive values OPEN and CLOSED, may have several values at once, and can be extended. The format must also identify the presentity, and must allow integrity, confidentiality and authentication to be applied.

Two features were added beyond that model: a relative priority for contact addresses, and a timestamp for when the information was created. The timestamp lets a receiver know when data was created even if the message carrying it was delayed, and it helps detect replay attacks. XML was chosen because presence data is hierarchical and must be fully extensible, which made it preferable to alternatives such as vCard.
sections.eli5: The designers packed only what they really needed, like a lunchbox with just the essentials. They added two extras: which way to reach you first, and what time the note was written.

sections.title: The Structure of a PIDF Document
sections.content:
A PIDF object is a well-formed XML document. It MUST have the XML declaration and SHOULD include an encoding declaration. If a MIME charset parameter is present and differs from the encoding declaration, the parameter wins. Every conformant application MUST accept UTF-8.

The root is a <presence> element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf. It MUST carry an entity attribute holding the pres URL of the presentity publishing the document. Inside it come any number of <tuple> elements, then any number of <note> elements, then optional extension elements from other namespaces.

Each <tuple> MUST have an id attribute that is unique among the tuples of the same presentity. It contains a mandatory <status>, optional extension elements, an optional <contact>, any number of <note> elements and an optional <timestamp>. Tuples let a sender segment information, for example when it comes from different devices or was generated at different times, and the RFC says tuples should be preferred over creating multiple PIDF instances.

The <status> element must have at least one child. This memo defines only <basic>, whose value is the string open or closed. For instant messaging these mean that the contact's instant inbox is ready, or unable, to accept an instant message. A tuple with a <basic> status SHOULD also contain a <contact>, and tuples MAY contradict each other.

The <contact> element holds a URL and may have a priority attribute: a decimal number from 0 to 1 inclusive with at most 3 digits after the decimal point, where higher means more preferred. If it is omitted the address gets the lowest priority. The <note> element is a human-readable comment about the presentity (as a child of <presence>) or about one tuple. It SHOULD NOT be used as a non-interoperable substitute for status, and SHOULD carry an xml:lang attribute. The <timestamp> follows RFC 3339, and a presentity MUST NOT generate successive <presence> elements with the same timestamp.
sections.eli5: A PIDF note is like a card with a name on top and a few small boxes under it. Each box says open or closed, how to reach you, a short message and when it was written.

sections.title: Extending Status with Namespaces
sections.content:
Extensibility is built on XML namespaces. Extensions MUST NOT change how <basic> is understood, nor the structure or meaning of PIDF bodies. They only add richer data. A namespace URI is used as a globally unique name, and it must be a full absolute URI; it does not have to be fetchable.

The default rule is forgiving: a processor MUST ignore any element with an unrecognized name, including everything inside it. The exception is the mustUnderstand attribute ('true' or '1'), which marks a nested element as required for a complex extension. If a <status> block holds an unrecognized element marked this way, the whole element is treated as unrecognized and not processed. To keep minimal implementations safe, mustUnderstand MUST be used only inside optional elements nested in a <status>, so a failed extension does not break the basic information.

New status values, such as a location, are added next to <basic>. A status that adds values like 'away', 'busy' or 'offline' must still include <basic>, so older agents keep working, and extensions need not map each value to open or closed.

Standardized status extensions live under the umbrella namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:status, and new values under it MUST be defined by a standards-track RFC. Such an RFC must supply an XML Schema, register the extension name with IANA, and discuss the extension's domain of applicability and the semantics of its states. It SHOULD also explain how its states relate to <basic>.
sections.eli5: If you want to add a new box to the card, like where you are, you put it in with a clearly labeled sticker. Readers who do not know the sticker skip it, so old readers never get confused.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows the same simple document twice: once with a prefix (impp:) and once with a default namespace. Both mean the same thing, because the prefix is arbitrary and the namespace URI defines the naming scope.

A longer example has two tuples. The first has status open, an extension element for instant messaging status (busy), an extension element for location (home), a contact with priority 0.8, notes in English and French, and a timestamp. The second is an open mailto contact with priority 1.0, and a presentity-level note follows. A further example marks myex:ex1 with mustUnderstand: if it is not recognized, the enclosing myex:complexExtension MUST be ignored, while the other unrecognized elements MAY be ignored.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample cards already filled in, so you can see exactly where each piece goes.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
Presence is very privacy-sensitive, so the protocol carrying PIDF MUST be able to protect it from eavesdropping, corruption, tampering and replay. These protections must work end to end, even when a gateway sits between presence systems. Since PIDF has its own MIME type, the RFC finds MIME-level protection with S/MIME appropriate, following the core CPP specification.

Timestamps give some rudimentary replay protection. A watcher SHOULD ignore outdated presence information, for instance when the newest timestamp is older than the newest one in the last information received. The RFC suggests, as an example only, that information more than one hour old could be considered outdated.

For internationalization, all conformant processors MUST generate and accept UTF-8, and are strongly discouraged from emitting any other encoding.
sections.eli5: Where you are is private, so the note needs a lock. The time written on it also helps spot someone replaying an old note pretending it is fresh.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to register three things. The first is the media type application/pidf+xml, which follows the conventions of RFC 3023, including the +xml suffix. It has an optional charset parameter, which is RECOMMENDED, and UTF-8 is the default.

The other two are XML namespace URNs: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf for the elements in this document, and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:status for standardized status extensions. The media type registration lists its intended usage as limited use.
sections.eli5: Registering is like putting the new card layout in the official list of layouts, so everyone can look up its name and rules.

viz.caption: ELEMENT HIERARCHY OF A PIDF DOCUMENT
SIMPLE PIDF DOCUMENT WITH A DEFAULT NAMESPACE (RFC 3863)

data.title: Minimal presence document
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<presence xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf"
    entity="pres:someone@example.com">
  <tuple id="sg89ae">
    <status>
      <basic>open</basic>
    </status>
    <contact priority="0.8">tel:+09012345678</contact>
  </tuple>
</presence>
